Predict from a GWR spatial model

Source: R/model-classes.R
predict.gwr_fit.Rd

When newdata is NULL, returns the in-sample fitted values. Otherwise solves one local regression at each new location, with the fit's kernel and bandwidth (an adaptive bandwidth counts neighbours among the training points), and returns \(x^\top\hat\beta(u)\). The local regressions are weighted least squares solved by a pivoted QR, the solve fit_gwr_model() uses; on a window of full rank the values equal those of GWmodel::gwr.predict() to rounding error, and at a training location with that row's own predictors they equal fitted(). Each location stands alone: one that cannot be estimated does not affect the others. newdata is first transformed to the CRS used during fitting (via ensure_projected()), so predictions are computed in a single coordinate system regardless of the CRS newdata arrives in.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'gwr_fit'
predict(object, newdata = NULL, se.fit = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

object

A gwr_fit object.

newdata

An sf object with the same predictors. The response variable need not be present (true out-of-sample prediction is supported). NULL = fitted values.

se.fit

Logical; also return standard errors. Default FALSE.

...

Ignored.

Value

With se.fit = FALSE, a numeric vector aligned to nrow(newdata), with NA for rows dropped as missing or non-finite, and for locations whose local regression cannot be estimated (see When a prediction is NA); a warning counts those. If the design matrix for newdata cannot be built, every value is NA and a warning says why. CRS-less newdata first receives the interpretation the training data got, so the same rows land where they did at fit time.

With se.fit = TRUE, a list: fit (that vector), se.fit (the standard error of the fitted value, \(\hat\sigma\sqrt{s^\top s}\) with \(s\) the weights the local regression puts on the training responses), se.pred (the standard error of a new observation there, \(\hat\sigma\sqrt{1 + s^\top s}\), the square root of GWmodel::gwr.predict()'s prediction variance), residual.scale (\(\hat\sigma\), from the fit's residual sum of squares over its effective degrees of freedom) and df (those degrees of freedom). The standard errors treat the bandwidth as known and the local model as true at each location; they do not measure the bias of a local fit and are NA where the prediction is.

When a prediction is NA

A prediction is returned when it is estimable from the training points that carry weight at the new location, and is NA otherwise:

  • no training point carries weight there (a location beyond a fixed bisquare, tricube or boxcar bandwidth);

  • the training points in the window cannot place the new row: a predictor is constant among them at a value other than the new row's (a regional indicator, at a location whose window lies wholly in another region), or fewer of them carry weight than the new row needs.

Where a predictor is constant in the window at the new row's own value, its coefficient is not needed and the prediction is returned. The decision uses the rule and the tolerance of the fit (see fit_gwr_model, The local solve). A warning of class "spatialkit_gwr_not_estimable" counts the NA predictions.

Locations beyond the reach of the fit

An adaptive bandwidth always finds its neighbours, and a Gaussian or an exponential kernel weights every training point, so a location far from the data still gets a number: the local regression of training points that are all far away, extrapolated. When a new location's nearest training point is farther than the widest kernel used at any training location reaches, the prediction is returned and a warning of class "spatialkit_gwr_extrapolation" counts those locations and gives the range of their distances. The widest kernel is the largest distance from a training point to its bandwidth-th nearest neighbour (object$info$max_kernel_width), or the bandwidth itself when it is fixed. A bisquare, tricube or boxcar kernel reaches as far as its width; a Gaussian or exponential kernel has no edge, and its reach is taken as three widths. The check is on distance alone and is lenient: a location just outside the data is not flagged.

The warning is raised once per call, with that call's counts. predict_surface(), which predicts a grid in chunks, and cv_gwr() and cv_spatial(), which predict fold by fold, collect the warnings of their pieces and raise one under their own name, with the totals and the number of calls they are over (calls). The folds of a cross-validation are separate fits, so a cross-validation gives the smallest and the largest reach among them. cv_block_size_sweep() and select_features_forward() run many cross-validations of one learner and raise one warning for the sweep. A sweep predicts the same rows from several fits, so its totals count a location once for each fit that put it out of reach, and the message says so. model_metrics(fit, newdata) is one call and raises the warning once. A loop of your own over predict() gets one warning per call; the condition carries its numbers as fields (n_far, n, reach, and nearest, the smallest and largest distance to a nearest training point), so a handler can total them: withCallingHandlers(..., spatialkit_gwr_extrapolation = function(w) { total <<- total + w$n_far; invokeRestart("muffleWarning") }). To drop it where extrapolation is intended, use suppressWarnings(predict(fit, newdata), classes = "spatialkit_gwr_extrapolation"). The warning that counts NA predictions (class "spatialkit_gwr_not_estimable") carries n_na, n and n_empty and is collected the same way.
